description: Capability evals for the experimental-design skill. Seven tasks spanning the full design workflow: A/B test briefs, scoped sample-size questions, design critiques, quasi-experiments, interference problems, and file-based power calculations. Assertions are objectively checkable properties a well-guided response should have.

evals.name: checkout-ab-full-brief
evals.prompt: We're launching a redesigned checkout flow and want to run an experiment. Current purchase-completion rate at the cart is roughly 3%, and we get about 40,000 cart sessions per week. Walk me through designing this experiment end-to-end.
evals.expected_output: A full design brief covering: randomization unit (user, not session), ITT estimand, guardrail metrics (revenue per session, latency, error rate), sample-size calculation via the script for a stated MDE, runtime in whole weeks, no-peeking stopping rule (and the >30% false-positive rate warning if peeking), novelty-effect mitigation (≥2 weeks), SRM check, and an open-decisions section.

assertions.text: Randomizes by user (not session), explaining that session-level randomization would expose the same user to both flows
Asks for or states a specific MDE and runs the bundled script (power_analysis.py) to produce the required N per arm — does NOT report a sample size from mental math alone
Specifies guardrail metrics beyond the primary (e.g. revenue per session, latency, or payment-error rate)
States a fixed stopping rule and warns that peeking against a fixed test can push the real false-positive rate well above 5% (e.g. '>30%' or 'dramatically')
Recommends running at least two full weeks and mentions novelty effect or weekly seasonality as the reason
Mentions an SRM (sample-ratio mismatch) check before reading results
Frames the analysis as ITT (intent-to-treat) on the triggered population
Includes a section or note on open decisions the user still needs to make (e.g. the MDE threshold)

evals.name: scoped-sample-size-onboarding
evals.prompt: We're testing a new onboarding screen. Our baseline completion rate is 22%. We want to detect a 2-percentage-point absolute improvement (22% → 24%). How many users per arm do we need, assuming α=0.05 two-sided and 80% power?
evals.expected_output: A focused, short answer: ~6,950 users per arm (from the script), a note that '2pp' is being treated as absolute (and flagging what a 2% relative lift would cost), and a brief runtime translation. No unsolicited full brief.

assertions.text: Reports approximately 6,950 users per arm (within ±200 of the script output), derived from running power_analysis.py, not from a formula quoted inline
Clarifies the absolute vs. relative interpretation of '2 percentage points', noting the two interpretations give very different sample sizes
Translates the per-arm N to a runtime given daily traffic (or asks for traffic to do so)
Stays scoped — does not produce a full experiment brief when only sample size was asked

evals.name: critique-no-control-before-after
evals.prompt: We shipped a feed redesign to 100% of users last week. Active minutes went up 8% week-over-week. Our VP wants to use this as proof the redesign worked and greenlight more redesigns like it. Is this strong evidence?
evals.expected_output: A clear critique: no control group means no counterfactual, before-after comparisons absorb all other changes (seasonality, marketing, other releases), so the 8% cannot be attributed to the redesign. Offer the best available alternatives (holdback going forward, DiD if a comparable segment exists, ITS). Do not validate the causal claim.

assertions.text: States explicitly that the absence of a control group means there is no counterfactual, so the 8% cannot be attributed to the redesign
Names at least two concrete alternative explanations for the observed lift (e.g. seasonality, marketing push, other concurrent changes, day-of-week effects)
Does not endorse the VP's causal claim or frame the result as strong evidence
Offers at least one constructive path forward (holdback, diff-in-diff, interrupted time series, or staggered rollout)
Keeps ethics or moralizing proportionate — this is a low-stakes observational analysis, not a harm scenario

evals.name: within-subjects-navigation-study
evals.prompt: We're running a usability study comparing 3 navigation layouts. We can recruit about 30 participants. Each session measures task-completion time and error rate. How should we design this?
evals.expected_output: Recommends within-subjects (every participant sees all 3 layouts), explains that between-subjects with 10/cell is hopeless given person-to-person variance, specifies counterbalancing via Latin square, and requires mixed-effects analysis (random intercept per participant) for both outcomes. Honest about power limits.

assertions.text: Recommends a within-subjects design where every participant sees all three layouts
Explains WHY within-subjects: it removes between-person variance (each person is their own control), making n=30 feasible where between-subjects would not be
Specifies counterbalancing order across participants (Latin square or equivalent) to control for order and carryover effects
Specifies a repeated-measures analysis method (mixed-effects model, repeated-measures ANOVA, or equivalent) rather than treating the observations as independent
Is honest about the power limitation: 30 participants only reliably detects large within-person differences; a null is inconclusive, not proof of equivalence

evals.name: quasi-experiment-state-fee-cap
evals.prompt: California passed a fee cap law on January 1st. I have monthly state-level panel data for all 50 states for the past 3 years. How can I estimate the causal effect of the fee cap?
evals.expected_output: DiD as the primary method, with the parallel-trends assumption stated as the load-bearing caveat (and how to check it). Synthetic control recommended as a complement. Key threats named (concurrent CA-only shocks, anticipation, donor-state contamination). Suggests falsification. Does not claim randomization equivalence.

assertions.text: Recommends difference-in-differences (DiD) as the primary method, with California as treated and other states as comparison
Names the parallel-trends assumption as the key identifying assumption that DiD rests on, and explains how to check it (pre-period plot or formal test)
Suggests synthetic control as a complement or alternative, noting it is purpose-built for a single treated unit
Names at least one concrete threat specific to this design (e.g. concurrent CA-only shock, anticipation effects, other states passing similar laws)
Recommends a falsification or placebo check (e.g. placebo date, placebo outcome, or permutation inference)

evals.name: social-interference-cluster-randomization
evals.prompt: We're building a 'what your friends are watching' recommendation feature. We want to A/B test it with a standard 50/50 user-level random split. My colleague says this will give us a biased answer. Who is right?
evals.expected_output: Colleague is right. A user-level split violates SUTVA because treated users affect control users through the social graph, diluting the measured effect. Fix: cluster-randomize by social community. Name the power cost (design effect from ICC). Recommend sizing with --icc / --cluster-size flags.

assertions.text: States the colleague is correct and explains WHY: the feature creates interference (SUTVA violation) because treated users affect control-group users through the social graph
Explains the direction of bias: spillover from treated to control dilutes the measured effect, causing underestimation of the true treatment effect
Recommends cluster randomization at the level of social communities (or ego-network / geo clusters as fallback)
Warns about the power cost: within-cluster correlation (ICC) inflates the design effect and reduces effective sample size, so the test will need more units than a naive user-level calculation implies
Suggests using the power script's cluster options (--icc / --cluster-size) or equivalent to size the test correctly under the design effect

evals.name: file-based-power-from-csv
evals.prompt: I've attached checkout_history.csv — it has 63 days of daily sessions and conversions for our payment step. We want to run an A/B test targeting a 5% relative lift. Use the file to compute the required sample size and estimate how long the test would need to run.
evals.expected_output: Reads the CSV, computes ~4.1% baseline conversion and ~4,600 sessions/day, runs the script with --mde 0.05 --relative to get ~149,000-150,000/arm, translates to ~9-10 weeks at 50/50 split, flags the long runtime and names variance reduction (CUPED) and MDE reconsideration as the key levers, mentions weekly seasonality requiring whole-week runs.

assertions.text: Reads the CSV file to derive baseline conversion rate and average daily traffic — does not ask the user to supply these numbers manually

Runs power_analysis.py with --mde 0.05 --relative (or equivalent) on the computed baseline to get approximately 149,000-150,000 per arm (exact value depends on computed baseline; accept any result in the 145K–155K range)
Translates N to a runtime estimate using the traffic from the file, arriving at approximately 9-10 weeks
Flags that the runtime is long and names CUPED / variance reduction as a lever to shorten it
Notes the visible weekday/weekend seasonality and recommends whole-week runs to avoid confounding
